```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Load the cleaned deer dataset
library(readr)
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

df_deer_clean <- read_csv("data/processed/NC_Deer_Cleaned_2010_2020.csv")
NC_map <- st_read("data/processed/NC_map_joined.shp")

# Check the dataset
dim(df_deer_clean)
head(df_deer_clean)
```

## Figures and Maps
```{r counting observations by year}
# Count deer observations by year
annual_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(df_deer_clean$year)
)

# Rename columns
names(annual_counts) <- c("Year", "Observations")

# Convert year and count to numeric
annual_counts$Year <- as.integer(
  as.character(annual_counts$Year)
)

annual_counts$Observations <- as.integer(
  annual_counts$Observations
)

# View the summary table
annual_counts

```

```{r figure 1}

# Figure 1: Annual white-tailed deer observations in NC

plot(
  annual_counts$Year,
  annual_counts$Observations,
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = "steelblue",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Number of observations",
  main = "Annual White-tailed Deer Observations in North Carolina",
  xaxt = "n"
)

axis(
  1,
  at = 2010:2020,
  labels = 2010:2020
)
```

### Figure 1. Annual White-tailed Deer Observations in North Carolina (2010–2020)
Question: How did the number of recorded white-tailed deer observations change from 2010 to 2020?
Observed pattern: The annual number of observations increased (12 records in 2010 to 1,048 in 2020).
Units: Number of iNaturalist observation records per year.
Limitation: The observed numbers do not equate to the actual number of deer populations. This trend may merely indicate an increase in people's participation on the iNaturalist platform, rather than an actual growth in the deer population.

```{r assign the deer observations to the counties}
# Load North Carolina county boundaries
nc_map <- st_read("data/processed/NC_map_joined.shp")

# Convert deer coordinates into spatial points
deer_sf <- st_as_sf(
  df_deer_clean,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

# Match the coordinate system of the county map
deer_sf <- st_transform(deer_sf, st_crs(NC_map))

# Assign each deer observation to a county
deer_county <- st_join(
  deer_sf,
  NC_map[, c("NAME", "GEOID")],
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

# Preview the results
head(st_drop_geometry(deer_county)[, c("id", "NAME", "GEOID")])
```

```{r figure 2}
# Count deer observations by county
county_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(deer_county$NAME)
)

# Rename columns
names(county_counts) <- c("NAME", "deer_count")

# Convert counts to numeric
county_counts$deer_count <- as.integer(county_counts$deer_count)

# Preview
head(county_counts)

# Join deer counts to county boundaries
NC_map$deer_count <- county_counts$deer_count[
  match(NC_map$NAME, county_counts$NAME)
]

# Counties with no observations should have a count of zero
NC_map$deer_count[is.na(NC_map$deer_count)] <- 0

# Figure 2: Deer observations by county
plot(
  NC_map["deer_count"],
  main = "White-tailed Deer Observations by County in NC",
  pal = colorRampPalette(c("lightblue", "darkblue")),
  key.pos = 4,
  axes = FALSE,
  reset = FALSE
)
```

### Figure 2. Spatial Distribution of White-tailed Deer Observations by County in North Carolina (2010–2020)
Question: How are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties?
Observed pattern: Deer observations were unevenly distributed across counties.
Units: Number of iNaturalist deer observation records per county.
Limitation: Observation counts were not adjusted for county area or differences in observer. Additionally, 33 observations could not be assigned to a county and were excluded from this map. Therefore, higher observation counts do not necessarily indicate higher deer population density.

```{r summary table}

# Summary table for all 100 counties
all_counties <- data.frame(
  County = NC_map$NAME,
  Observations = NC_map$deer_count
)

# Sort from highest to lowest
all_counties <- all_counties[
  order(-all_counties$Observations),
]

knitr::kable(
  all_counties,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Deer Observations by County (2010–2020)"
)

# Top 10 counties by deer observations

county_top10 <- county_counts[
  order(county_counts$deer_count, decreasing = TRUE),
][1:10, ]

# Add ranking
county_top10 <- data.frame(
  Rank = 1:10,
  County = county_top10$NAME,
  Observations = county_top10$deer_count
)

# Display as a formatted table
knitr::kable(
  county_top10,
  caption = "Top 10 NC Counties by White-tailed Deer Observations (2010–2020)",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Horizontal bar chart for top 10 counties
par(mar = c(5, 12, 4, 2))

barplot(
  rev(county_top10$Observations),
  names.arg = rev(county_top10$County),
  horiz = TRUE,
  las = 1,
  col = "steelblue",
  cex.names = 0.8,
  xlab = "Number of observations",
  main = "Top 10 Counties by Deer Observations"
)

```

### Three main findings
Temporal increase: Deer observation records increased substantially from 2010 to 2020, especially after 2016.
Uneven spatial distribution: Observations were not evenly distributed across North Carolina counties.
Concentration in a few counties: Wake (547), Orange (265), and Durham (188) together accounted for approximately 35% of county-assigned observations.

```{r data Wrangling}
df_deer_spatial <- df_deer_clean %>%
  select(observed_on, year, longitude, latitude) %>%
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c('longitude','latitude'), crs=4269)
df_deer_in_NC <- st_join(df_deer_spatial, NC_map, join = st_within) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(development = ifelse(HU_dif > 0, "yes", "no"),
         forest = ifelse(VEG_dif < 0, "dec", "inc")) %>%
  group_by(NAME, year, development, forest) %>%
  summarise(observation=n()) %>%
  ungroup(year, development, forest) %>%
  mutate(period = ifelse(year == "2016" | year == "2017" | year == "2018" | year == "2019", NA, 
                         ifelse(year == "2020", "after", "before")))
```

```{r map 1}
map_deer_in_NC = ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = NC_map, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5, aes(fill = HU_dif)) + 
  geom_sf(data = df_deer_spatial%>%filter(year == "2010" | year == "2011" | year == "2012" | year == "2013" | year == "2014" | year == "2015"), color = "cyan", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, stroke = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="darkblue", high="red") +
  labs(title = "Housing Unit Differnce by Counties with White-tailed Deer Observations before Development",
       fill = "Difference",
       caption = "Housing unit difference is calculated with data from 2020 subtracting data from 2010. Deer observation is the sum from 2010\nto 2015. The blue means unchanged or small increase of housing units in the counties, and the red means large increase.") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11.5),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0))
map_deer_in_NC
```

### Map 1-4
Question: How are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties with different development rate?
Observed pattern: In terms of housing units, the deer observations before the development (2010-2015) spread out more than the once from 2020, which gather in 4 clusters in the counties with more housing units. For vegetation cover changes, the pattern is less obvious: deer observations cluster in both regions with high and low destruction.
Units: Number of iNaturalist deer observation records per county.
Limitation: There were fewer data for 2010 to 2015, so we decided to add all these years up and treat the sum as the pre-development deer distribution. Also, the increase in deer observation may not correlated to development itself, but the increase of people visiting the area and thus seeing more deer.

## ANOVA
```{r ANOVA Development}
model_dev <- aov(log(observation) ~ period + development + period*development, data = df_deer_in_NC)
TukeyHSD(model_dev)
```

```{r ANOVA Development Validity}
fit_dev <- model_dev$fitted
res_dev <- model_dev$res

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
boxplot(observation ~ development+period, data = df_deer_in_NC)
qqnorm(res_dev, datax = TRUE)
qqline(res_dev, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(x = seq(1:length(res_dev)), y = res_dev, xlab="Order", ylab="Residuals")
lines(x = seq(1:length(res_dev)), y = res_dev)
abline(0,0)
plot(fit_dev, res_dev, xlab="Fitted Values", ylab="Residuals")
```

```{r ANOVA Forest}
model_forest <- aov(log(observation) ~ period + forest + period*forest, data = df_deer_in_NC)
summary(model_forest)
TukeyHSD(model_forest)
```

```{r ANOVA Forest Validity}
fit_forest <- model_forest$fitted
res_forest <- model_forest$res

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
boxplot(observation ~ forest+period, data = df_deer_in_NC)
qqnorm(res_forest, datax = TRUE)
qqline(res_forest, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(x = seq(1:length(res_forest)), y = res_forest, xlab="Order", ylab="Residuals")
lines(x = seq(1:length(res_forest)), y = res_forest)
abline(0,0)
plot(fit_forest, res_forest, xlab="Fitted Values", ylab="Residuals")
```

### ANOVA analysis
Question: Are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties significantly different between counties with different development rate?
We marked the deer observations from 2010-2015 as pre-development and the data from 2020 as post-development. To fit the ANOVA assumptions better, according to the validity plots, the data is natural log transformed. 
For housing units, development, period, and their interaction are all significant on deer observation. The Tukey test shows that before the development, the deer observation does not have a significant difference in distribution across the counties. This is the only insignificant case. By contrast, after the development, the deer observation shows a significant difference in distribution across the counties with high and low development.
For vegetation cover, forest clearing, period, and their interaction are all significant on deer observation. The Tukey test shows that vegetation cover before development does not have a significant difference on deer observation distribution. However, counties with decreased vegetation cover has a significant difference on deer observation distribution before and after the development. Moreover, after the development, the level of vegetation destruction is significant on deer observation distribution.
